In [[nonstandard analysis]], a field of mathematics, the '''increment theorem''' states the following: Suppose a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] {{math|1=''y'' = ''f''(''x'')}} is [[Differentiable function|differentiable]] at {{mvar|x}} and that {{math|Δ''x''}} is [[infinitesimal]]. Then
<math display="block">\Delta y = f'(x)\,\Delta x + \varepsilon\, \Delta x</math>
for some infinitesimal {{mvar|ε}}, where
<math display="block">\Delta y=f(x+\Delta x)-f(x).</math>

If <math display="inline">\Delta x \neq 0</math> then we may write
<math display="block">\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = f'(x) + \varepsilon,</math>
which implies that <math display="inline">\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\approx f'(x)</math>, or in other words that <math display="inline"> \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}</math> is infinitely close to <math display="inline"> f'(x)</math>, or <math display="inline"> f'(x)</math> is the [[standard part function|standard part]] of <math display="inline"> \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}</math>.

A similar theorem exists in standard Calculus.  Again assume that {{math|1=''y'' = ''f''(''x'')}} is differentiable, but now let {{math|Δ''x''}} be a nonzero standard real number. Then the same equation
<math display="block">\Delta y = f'(x)\,\Delta x + \varepsilon\, \Delta x</math>
holds with the same definition of {{math|Δ''y''}}, but instead of {{mvar|ε}} being infinitesimal, we have
<math display="block"> \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \varepsilon = 0 </math>
(treating {{mvar|x}} and {{math|''f''}} as given so that {{mvar|ε}} is a function of {{math|Δ''x''}} alone).
